gloss: to attend to · to be in charge of · steward
formNote: The Shuowen explains 司 as 后 turned around. Early scribes could write graphs facing either way, so the two are sometimes hard to tell apart; the graph’s deeper origin is unknown.
summary: The steward’s verb: to attend to, to be responsible for. It names offices (司馬, master of horse; 司空, minister of works) and the duty of tending a trust well without overreaching it.
placement: High on the left wing, mirroring 愛 across the attractor.

satellites.title: A Mirror-Image Graph
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen defines 司 as “an official who manages affairs outside” and derives its shape from 后 reversed. Because early graphs could face either way, 司 and 后 are sometimes indistinguishable.
satellites.caveat: Hence the continuing debate over whether the great Shang cauldron reads 司母戊 or 后母戊.

cites.locator: 司母戊 / 后母戊 ding

satellites.title: Keeper of an Office
satellites.evidence: 司命 is the deity who keeps the span of life; 有司 are the officers in charge of particular matters. In both, 司 is accountable care for a specific trust.

cites.locator: 九歌: 大司命, 少司命

satellites.title: Tending a Domain
satellites.evidence: Malay mengelola and mengurus — to manage, look after, put in order — carry the same sense of responsible tending rather than command.

satellites.title: Steering, Not Forcing
satellites.evidence: Greek κυβερνάω, “to steer a ship”, is the root of govern and cybernetics; French présider is “to sit before”, to preside. Like 司, both picture authority as attentive steering.
